title: PsExec-delivered python.exe payload on nashua is lateral movement, not sniffing
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran PsExec64.exe with explicit credentials (dmevals\pbeesly) against \\NASHUA to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, which then ran on nashua.dmevals.local under PSEXESVC.exe and made repeated outbound TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. This is credential-based lateral movement / C2, not network sniffing; no capture driver or sniffing tool was involved. Reported here only because it appeared in the T1040 hunt scope.

title: Reflective in-memory API resolution (GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle) via PowerShell on scranton
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block (Event 4104, ScriptBlockId bc19aae2-d1f9-49b2-b718-192531ae928f) that reflectively resolves native APIs: it fetches Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods from System.dll, calls GetModuleHandle/GetProcAddress, defines a dynamic assembly named 'ReflectedDelegate' with a delegate type, and then decodes a base64 shellcode blob ([System.Convert]::FromBase64String("/EiD5PDozAAAA...")) for in-memory execution. This is the classic pattern for hooking/intercepting native credential APIs without touching disk. It is preceded by a hidden base64-encoded PowerShell launch (powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -e ...) and a steganographic loader reading C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png into IEX.

title: No MFA interception artifacts; observed credential activity is explicit-credential logon (PsExec lateral movement)
summary: Hunting for T1111 (MFA Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and windows.powershell found no evidence of MFA/smart-card/token interception. The 4648 explicit-credential logons on nashua.dmevals.local and scranton.dmevals.local show the account pbeesly's credentials being used by C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec service) and svchost.exe targeting 'localhost' — this is credential USE for lateral movement, not interception of an MFA factor. Logon types are ordinary (2 interactive, 3 network, 5 service, 10 RDP). The only 'Credential'-named registry writes are benign Windows components: lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to 0x0 (Credential Guard not enabled) and services.exe registering the built-in CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service. Registry 'Token' hits are all Windows ContentManagementSDK\DeviceTokens\MSA writes by backgroundTaskHost.exe (normal OS behavior). No smartcard/MFA/token command lines or credential-provider tampering were observed.

On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:35:25 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) connected to 192.168.0.4 over SMB (tcp/445 and tcp/139) and then issued 36 HTTP requests to port 80 using the Windows WebDAV redirector user agents 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and 'DavClnt'. The requests were OPTIONS and PROPFIND to /webdav, /webdav/, /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe. The PROPFIND requests carried an AUTHORIZATION header (client_header_names includes AUTHORIZATION) and the server answered 401 Unauthorized before returning 207 Multi-Status, i.e. the host's credentials were coerced and accepted by the remote WebDAV listener. This is the classic T1187 forced-authentication chain (SMB/WebDAV UNC trigger -> NTLM credential capture) against an attacker-controlled listener at 192.168.0.4. All 36 WebDAV requests originate from 10.0.1.4 and target 192.168.0.4 only.
title: WebDAV/SMB forced-authentication coercion from scranton (10.0.1.4) to 192.168.0.4

title: WebDAV DavSetCookie via rundll32/davclnt.dll on scranton (benign Windows WebDAV redirector)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly spawned rundll32.exe loading davclnt.dll with the DavSetCookie export five times (2020-05-02 03:08:50 and 03:10:22-03:10:23), parent process svchost.exe. The command line 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' is the Windows WebDAV redirector storing a WebDAV authentication cookie for the http://192.168.0.4/webdav share. This is a WebDAV client cookie, not a browser/web-application session cookie, and is normal Windows behaviour when a WebDAV path is accessed. No browser cookie store was read or exfiltrated.

title: PsExec-launched python.exe on nashua and WebDAV python.exe retrieval (lateral movement, not cookie theft)
summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe was launched repeatedly (2020-05-02 03:11:40-03:15:04) with parent C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe under user pbeesly, and Zeek shows HTTP GET /webdav/python.exe from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 with user-agent Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362. This is PsExec/WebDAV-delivered tooling consistent with lateral movement, but the command lines contain no cookie references and no browser cookie store was accessed, so it is not evidence of T1539 web session cookie theft.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script (readme.ps1 in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite) defining a Get-PrivateKeys function that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and exports every certificate with a thumbprint to a randomly-named .pfx file under the user's Downloads folder, protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. This is direct private-key/certificate theft (T1552.004). It is part of a larger intrusion chain on the same host/user: a .scr payload executed from C:\ProgramData\victim, PowerShell download/extraction of SysinternalsSuite, accesschk.exe credential hunting, and an Invoke-Exfil function that 7-Zip-compresses the Downloads folder with password 'lolol'.
